_readme: THE SURFACES A CLAIM MAY REST ON, NAMED ONCE.
`I searched` is not a method and `Microsoft says` is not a citation. Each
surface below answers a different question and none of them answers
another's, so a rule that consulted one has established what that one
THE RESPONSE OUTRANKS THE PROSE. Where a reference page and a tenant's own
answer disagree, the answer is what is true and the page is what somebody
intended. Both are recorded and the disagreement is the finding, which is
the capability this product is built on.
CURRENT DOCUMENTATION IS NOT THE WHOLE OF FIRST-PARTY EVIDENCE. Reference
pages say what the product does. They do not say what it is about to stop
doing, and a rule that was correct on the day it was written keeps being
published long after the day it stopped being. When an announced change
moves what an outcome MEANS, it is a source of the rule.
Asked BEFORE the rule is written, never after. `SPO-SCRIPT-001` was
written three times, and every rewrite was a surface that had not been

`where` is the list of places, and it is not a suggestion: a claim that cites none of them has cited nothing. Adding a place is a deliberate edit, reviewed like a schema, because a source list that grows by habit stops meaning anything.

surfaces.name: The API response itself
surfaces.settles: what is, in this tenant, at the moment it was read
where: the PowerShell modules that wrap them: Microsoft.Graph, ExchangeOnlineManagement, MicrosoftTeams, PnP.PowerShell

surfaces.name: Microsoft Learn reference
surfaces.settles: what a value means, and the documented limits of a control
surfaces.does_not_settle: whether it is about to change, or what a tenant holds

surfaces.name: Microsoft 365 service descriptions
surfaces.settles: what a plan includes, per licence
surfaces.does_not_settle: what a tenant actually holds or has assigned

surfaces.name: Microsoft Graph changelog
surfaces.settles: what the API gained or lost, with dates
surfaces.does_not_settle: what a portal shows, or when a portal caught up

surfaces.name: Message Center
surfaces.settles: what changes, with an effect date and any opt-out retirement
surfaces.does_not_settle: anything about a tenant that did not receive the post
surfaces.note: Tenant-scoped and publicly mirrored. The tenant's own centre is the primary.

surfaces.name: Microsoft 365 Roadmap
surfaces.settles: what is announced. A status, never a fact

surfaces.name: Retirement and deprecation notices
where: https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/  product-group posts announcing an end of support

surfaces.name: An administration portal
surfaces.settles: what an administrator is shown, which is what they believe
surfaces.does_not_settle: what is true. It renders a value through a interface written at a different time, sometimes over a second control that overrides the one on screen
surfaces.note: Never a basis for a rule. Read as the SECOND SURFACE, so that a divergence from the authoritative one can be recorded as evidence.

surfaces.name: Community documentation, blogs, samples and issues
surfaces.does_not_settle: anything a rule may rest on. It is where to look next, not what to cite
where: https://www.nuno-silva.net/  (weekly digest of the Tenant Admin newsletter; keeps the MC id, which is what makes it checkable)
https://www.andrewconnell.com/articles  (first-hand investigation; carries a method to run, not an id to look up)
surfaces.note:
A DIGEST THAT PRESERVES THE IDENTIFIER IS WORTH MORE THAN ONE THAT EXPLAINS WELL. The Tenant Admin newsletter reaches an administrator's own centre and nowhere public, so a change can be real, dated and unfindable by anyone outside the tenant that received it. A weekly digest that reproduces each entry as `MC1319213 | May 22 - ...` hands back the one thing that can then be read at its own address. That is the whole of its value and the whole of its licence: it tells this engine WHAT TO GO AND READ, and the reading happens at rank 2. What must never travel from a digest into a rule, a page or a finding is the digest's own summary -- several of them are generated by a model, and a paraphrase of a paraphrase is how a product ends up publishing a sentence Microsoft never wrote.

THERE ARE TWO WAYS OUT OF RANK 5 AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME ONE. A digest carries an IDENTIFIER, and the way out is to read that identifier at rank 2. A first-hand technical investigation carries an EXPERIMENT -- somebody ran the thing and wrote down what it did -- and the way out is to run it here, which lands at rank 1 as this engine's own observation. Neither is ever a basis, and the difference between them is not credibility. It is which escalation the reader owes before citing anything.

The second kind carries a decay the first does not. A message id is fixed and will read the same in five years; a published experiment was true against the platform on the day it ran, and the platform is the thing that changes. So an investigation is never cited for its conclusion. It is cited, if at all, for the METHOD, and the conclusion is re-established by running it.
